3.5 The Term Structure of Interest Rates

The yield curve

Section titled “The yield curve”

In 3.3 Bond Pricing, zero-coupon bonds of different maturities had different spot rates. The relation between interest rates and maturity for one issuer (usually the government) is the term structure of interest rates, and its graph is the yield curve. This lesson writes sns_nsn​ for the nnn-year spot rate and rtr_trt​ for the 1-year rate in year ttt (the first year’s r1=s1r_1 = s_1r1​=s1​ is known today; those of later years are not yet known).

The yield curve has several common shapes:

  • upward-sloping: long rates are above short rates; this is the most common shape;
  • flat: rates of all maturities are close;
  • inverted: long rates are below short rates (2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices);
  • humped: medium-term rates are highest, with lower rates at both ends.

Why does the curve take different shapes? The usual explanations involve three things: expectations about future short rates, compensation for the risk of holding long bonds, and supply and demand at different maturities. We discuss them in turn.

The expectations hypothesis

Section titled “The expectations hypothesis”

First suppose investors care only about expected returns, not about risk. An investor with a two-year horizon can buy a 2-year zero, or buy a 1-year zero and, when it matures, another 1-year zero. If the two approaches had different expected returns, everyone would choose the better one until they became equal:

(1+s2)2=(1+s1)(1+E[r2])(1 + s_2)^2 = (1 + s_1)(1 + E[r_2])(1+s2​)2=(1+s1​)(1+E[r2​])

E[r2]E[r_2]E[r2​] is the 1-year rate the market expects next year. For any maturity,

(1+sn)n=(1+s1)(1+E[r2])⋯(1+E[rn])(1 + s_n)^n = (1 + s_1)(1 + E[r_2]) \cdots (1 + E[r_n])(1+sn​)n=(1+s1​)(1+E[r2​])⋯(1+E[rn​])

so the nnn-year rate is the geometric average of the expected short rates of each year, roughly sn≈1n(s1+E[r2]+⋯+E[rn])s_n \approx \frac{1}{n}(s_1 + E[r_2] + \cdots + E[r_n])sn​≈n1​(s1​+E[r2​]+⋯+E[rn​]). Compared with the definition in 3.3 Bond Pricing, this says that forward rates are the expected future short rates:

ft−1,t=E[rt]f_{t-1,t} = E[r_t]ft−1,t​=E[rt​]

This is the expectations hypothesis. Under it, an upward-sloping curve means the market expects short rates to rise, and an inverted curve means it expects them to fall; Lesson 2.5 Exercises Question 5 and 2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices used this idea.

When the curve slopes upward, long bonds have higher yields. Under the expectations hypothesis, are long bonds the better choice for an investor with a 1-year horizon? Check C1 asks about this.

Check C1
The expectations hypothesis holds and the yield curve slopes upward. An investor with a 1-year horizon who buys a 2-year zero and sells it after a year has a higher expected return than if he simply bought a 1-year bill.
Think: under the expectations hypothesis, what 1-year rate does the market expect a year from now? What does the bond's expected price then make the expected one-year return equal to?

The term premium

Section titled “The term premium”

The expectations hypothesis ignores risk. 3.4 Interest Rate Risk showed that for an investor with a 1-year horizon, a 1-year bill is riskless, while the price of a long bond after a year depends on the rates at that time: it has price risk, and the longer the duration, the larger the risk. If most investors have short horizons and are risk-averse, they demand an extra expected return from long bonds. Then forward rates are above expected future short rates:

ft−1,t=E[rt]+ϕtf_{t-1,t} = E[r_t] + \phi_tft−1,t​=E[rt​]+ϕt​

ϕt\phi_tϕt​ is the term premium. The theory that the term premium is positive and rises with maturity is the liquidity premium theory. In that case, forward rates used as forecasts of future short rates are too high on average.

So a long rate is roughly the average expected short rate plus the term premium. Figure 3-1 draws the two parts separately.

Check C2
In Figure 3-1, set the expected long-run level to 3% (the market expects short rates to fall from 4%) and the year-10 term premium to 2 percentage points. The yield curve then:
How much does the term premium raise long yields? Compare the 10-year yield with the 1-year 4%.
Both the expected part and the term premium change with maturity, so the curve is not completely flat.
Does the term premium raise or lower long yields? Would it make a falling curve steeper?

The term premium can also be negative. The preferred habitat theory holds that different investors prefer different maturities. For example, money market funds and corporate cash management prefer short bonds, while some investors have needs that make long bonds a better fit. Investors will leave their preferred maturity, but only for compensation, so supply and demand at each maturity affect the term premium: when the government issues more long-term debt, the term premium rises; when the central bank buys long Treasuries through quantitative easing, it falls. Estimates from the New York Fed’s ACM model show that the US 10-year term premium was negative for most of the time from around 2016 to the early 2020s. Which investors would hold long bonds at lower yields? Check C3 discusses an example.

Check C3
A pension fund must pay a large sum in 30 years. For it, which asset is the least risky?
With rolling 1-year bills, the money in 30 years depends on every future year's rate. What does that mean for a payment due in 30 years?
A money market fund's return moves with short rates, so the amount in 30 years is just as uncertain.
Stock values swing widely, so the amount in 30 years is even less certain and does not match a fixed payment.

Shapes of the curve and what they mean

Section titled “Shapes of the curve and what they mean”

The yield curve contains two kinds of information at the same time: the market’s expectations of future short rates, and the term premium. The term premium cannot be observed directly; it can only be estimated with models, and estimates from different models can differ a lot.

  • The US Treasury yield curve slopes upward most of the time, and on average long Treasuries yield more than short ones, which is consistent with a term premium that is positive on average.
  • Inversions usually follow sharp rate increases by the central bank: short rates are high, and the market expects cuts later (2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices).
  • Most movements of the curve can be described by three kinds of change: level, a shift of the whole curve up or down; slope, a change in the spread between long and short rates; and curvature, a change in medium-term rates relative to both ends. Litterman and Scheinkman (1991) found that these three explain most of the variation in US Treasury returns.
  • Must long rates fall when the central bank cuts its rate? Exercises Question 3 discusses this question.

For investors, extending duration earns the term premium on average but carries price risk. A common practice is “riding the yield curve”: when the curve slopes upward, buy bonds longer than the investment horizon and sell them before maturity. If the curve does not change, the bond’s remaining maturity shortens over time, its yield moves down along the curve, and its price rises. Under what conditions does this earn more? Check C4

Check C4
The expectations hypothesis holds and the yield curve slopes upward. Buying bonds longer than the investment horizon and selling them before maturity (riding the yield curve) has a higher expected return than buying bonds that match the horizon.
Think: under the expectations hypothesis, how does the market expect the yield curve to change over a year? Will the yield at sale still fall along today's curve?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The term structure of interest rates is the relation between rates and maturity for one issuer, shown by the yield curve; common shapes are upward-sloping, flat, inverted and humped.
  • Expectations hypothesis: (1+sn)n=(1+s1)(1+E[r2])⋯(1+E[rn])(1 + s_n)^n = (1 + s_1)(1 + E[r_2]) \cdots (1 + E[r_n])(1+sn​)n=(1+s1​)(1+E[r2​])⋯(1+E[rn​]); forward rates equal expected future short rates.
  • Term premium: ft−1,t=E[rt]+ϕtf_{t-1,t} = E[r_t] + \phi_tft−1,t​=E[rt​]+ϕt​. The liquidity premium theory holds that it is positive and rises with maturity; the preferred habitat theory holds that it depends on supply and demand at each maturity and can be positive or negative.
  • A long rate is roughly the average expected short rate plus the term premium; most movements of the curve can be described by changes in level, slope and curvature.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
The 1-, 2- and 3-year Treasury spot rates are 3%, 3.5% and 4%.
(a) Find the forward rates for years 2 and 3, f1,2f_{1,2}f1,2​ and f2,3f_{2,3}f2,3​. Under the expectations hypothesis, how does the market expect short rates to change?
(b) Suppose the term premiums in these forward rates are 0.5 and 1 percentage point. What 1-year rates does the market expect in years 2 and 3? How does this compare with the conclusion in (a)?
Question 2
The yield curve is flat at 4%, and the market expects next year's 1-year rate to be 4% as well.
(a) A 1-year investor buys a 2-year zero with face value 100 and sells it after a year. If next year's 1-year rate is 5% or 3%, what is his return in each case? How does this compare with buying a 1-year bill?
(b) If most investors invest for only 1 year and are risk-averse, will the 2-year yield still be 4%? What if most investors must make a payment in 2 years?
Question 3
The 1-year Treasury yield is 5% and the 10-year yield 4.3%. A model estimates the term premium in the 10-year yield at 0.5 percentage points.
(a) A commentator says: "The 10-year yield is 0.7 percentage points below the 1-year yield, so the market expects short rates over the next 10 years to average about 0.7 percentage points below today's." Roughly what average short rate does the market expect over the next 10 years? Does the commentator overstate or understate the expected fall in rates, and why?
(b) A year later, the central bank has cut its policy rate by 1 percentage point, yet the 10-year yield has risen. Give two possible explanations.
Question 4
The central bank announces large purchases of long-term Treasuries (quantitative easing, 2.5 Monetary Policy). This is estimated to lower the term premium in the 10-year yield by 0.5 percentage points, with expected short rates unchanged.
(a) Roughly how does the value of a long Treasury fund with modified duration 9 change? Under the pure expectations hypothesis, can such purchases lower long rates? Why does the preferred habitat theory say they can?
(b) If the purchases also convince the market that short rates will stay low for longer (forward guidance), through what other channel do long rates fall?
